selected_modules.reason: The issue is about preprocessing behavior and diagnostics for defining/undefining keywords as macros, with most reproducer cases doing preprocess-only runs and using C-family options like -Wkeyword-macro, -pedantic-errors, and -fmodules. The shared C-family module explicitly owns cpplib lexer/preprocessing infrastructure, shared option processing and predefined macros, and reusable diagnostics for C/C++ front ends, making it the strongest match for keyword-macro warning semantics.

The bug summary is specifically marked [C++26] P2843R3 and many reproducer cases are C++-only, including modules, coroutines, templates, and newer keywords like likely/co_await/concept/constexpr. The C++ front end owns C++ language rules, newer language features, modules support, and C++-specific diagnostics, so C++26 keyword classification and pedantic handling are likely to involve this module in addition to shared preprocessing logic.

The reproducer also contains many C23 preprocess-only cases checking warnings for C keywords such as _Alignas, _BitInt, _Thread_local, alignas, constexpr, etc. The C front end owns GNU C language rules and C-specific semantic/diagnostic behavior, so C23-specific keyword status and any front-end contribution to macro-warning classification can plausibly reside here.

Observed behavior and tests revolve around the new warning option -Wkeyword-macro plus pedantic modes across standards (-std=c23, -std=c++26). The options module owns declarative option definitions and runtime decoding/handling of warnings, aliases, and propagated option state, so adding or wiring a new warning like -Wkeyword-macro is highly likely to involve this module.

selected_files.reason: Best match for the observed surface failure that many reproducer cases use a new warning option (-Wkeyword-macro) and newer standards (-std=c23, -std=c++26 / c++2c). Since the runs currently fail at unrecognized options and the bug centers on warning/standard-gated preprocessing behavior across both C and C++, this file is a prime place for wiring option state into the front end/preprocessor.

Highly relevant declarative upstream source for the new warning switch itself. The reproducer and tests are built around -Wkeyword-macro, and the log shows it is currently unrecognized in several C and C++ cases. c.opt defines C-family command-line switches, aliases, masks, metadata, and flag bindings that GCC generates into option handling, so adding or exposing -Wkeyword-macro would naturally require this file.

Strong match because the bug is about whether many identifiers are treated as keywords under different language standards and whether defining/undefining them as macros should diagnose. That makes it a likely upstream source for shared keyword classification interfaces consumed by the warning/preprocessor path.

Most reproducer cases are preprocess-only and the expected diagnostics are attached to macro definition/undefinition of keywords. c-lex.cc is the documented interface layer between cpplib and C-family lexer/parser logic, handling preprocessor callbacks, token streams, and source-location updates. That makes it a plausible intermediate mechanism where keyword tokens or preprocessor events are bridged into front-end diagnostics for #define/#undef handling across C and C++.

In the C++ module, identifier/keyword classification is the most direct upstream source for deciding whether a macro name should be treated as a language keyword in the current dialect.

The parser is a strong candidate because it owns the C++ grammar and token interpretation on top of the lexer, including newer language constructs called out by the reproducer such as coroutines, concepts, modules, and C++26-related tokens. If P2843R3 changes whether preprocessing names remain keywords or become ordinary identifiers for macro purposes, parser-facing token classification and dialect-sensitive grammar handling are likely consumers or enforcers of that state within `gcc/cp`.

Because the issue concerns preprocessing and keyword macro define/undef behavior in C++ with modules enabled, `module.cc` is a high-value intermediate mechanism where macro state and C++-specific preprocessing behavior can interact.
